sources.entry: TCMalloc: Thread-Caching Malloc - The design statement for per-CPU caches built on restartable sequences and a hugepage-aware back end for TLB reach.

summary.title: TCMalloc : Thread-Caching Malloc
summary.one_liner: TCMalloc's design explained: a three-tier allocator (front-end caches, middle-end transfer cache and central free list, back-end pageheap) with per-CPU or per-thread caching, spans and pagemap, and hugepage-aware memory management.
takeaways: TCMalloc has three layers: a lock-free front-end cache, a middle-end (transfer cache and central free list, mutex-protected per size-class) that refills it, and a back-end pageheap that talks to the OS.
Per-CPU mode gives each logical CPU its own cache and uses restartable sequences to avoid locks; per-thread mode was the original design but its memory scaled with thread count.
Small allocations are rounded to one of 60-80 size-classes, while large objects bypass the caches and go straight to the pageheap.
The hugepage-aware back-end manages memory in 2MiB chunks on x86 to reduce TLB misses, using filler, region and hugepage caches.
summary.summary: The page is the design document for TCMalloc, Google's alternative to the system malloc. It describes the allocator as three components: a front-end cache providing fast, mostly lock-free allocation (per-CPU or per-thread), a middle-end (transfer cache and central free list) that refills the front-end, and a back-end pageheap (legacy or hugepage-aware) that fetches and returns memory from the OS. It also explains size-classes, spans and the pagemap, restartable sequences used for per-CPU caches, and memory overhead and VSS/RSS behavior.
